children: In an interaction with BW Businessworld, Dr. Rajeev Gautam, President, HORIBA India and Senior Corporate Officer, HORIBA Ltd., Japan, speaks about CAFE III preparedness, India’s multi-technology mobility transition, hydrogen testing and safety gaps, battery dependence on China and the localisation of testing capabilities.

India’s automotive transition is increasingly taking a multi-technology route, with internal combustion engines, CNG, electric vehicles and hydrogen expected to coexist rather than one technology immediately replacing the others. This transition is also creating new requirements for testing, validation and safety infrastructure.

According to Dr. Rajeev Gautam, President, HORIBA India Pvt. Ltd. and Senior Corporate Officer, HORIBA Ltd., Japan, India already has significant automotive testing capabilities, but hydrogen remains an emerging area where the wider industry needs to build expertise and infrastructure.

In a conversation with BW Businessworld, Gautam says the industry could prepare for the proposed CAFE III requirements relatively quickly, while building a broader hydrogen-testing ecosystem could take another one to two years. Edited excerpts:
With CAFE III proposed for FY2027-28, what new testing and validation requirements will automakers face? Is India’s existing testing infrastructure equipped for the new norms?

I don’t think the industry is completely ready for CAFE III yet, but it is not very difficult. The capability is already there within the industry. HORIBA also has its testing centre in Chakan, Pune, and we are working on it.
We should be ready in around three to four months. The infrastructure is already there; a little tweaking has to be done because the measurement remains the same. So, it is possible.

India’s vehicle market is increasingly spread across petrol, diesel, CNG, hybrids and EVs rather than moving uniformly towards electrification. How does this affect the infrastructure and investment OEMs will need?
There are three broad pathways. We have conventional fuels such as petrol and diesel, then we have electrification, and hydrogen is the new technology that is coming.
The government is looking at hydrogen for heavy-duty applications such as trucks and buses because it is zero-emission at the point of use, with water vapour as the emission.

For two- and three-wheelers, the focus can be on electrification. For four-wheel passenger vehicles such as cars, I think CNG and gasoline will continue because we do not yet have the capability to move everything to one technology.

The government is therefore looking at all three, and the industry is preparing for all three. We have testing facilities. OEMs can bring their vehicles to us, we can test them, provide the required data and support their R&D.
The government has sanctioned hydrogen mobility pilots covering fuel-cell and hydrogen internal combustion e
ngine technologies. Which applications in India can actually make a commercial case for hydrogen over battery-electric technology?
The problem with hydrogen is the cost. Hydrogen production is expensive today. India cannot afford hydrogen at those levels; we need to bring the cost down substantially, potentially to around $1–2.
That can happen when production volumes increase. The government and various industries are working towards that.

Electrification will continue, but batteries are also a constraint. Whatever batteries and materials are available to us largely come from outside. Battery-electric technology can cater to two- and three-wheelers, but for buses and other heavy-duty applications, you need much larger batteries. That becomes difficult.
India is targeting five million metric tonnes of green hydrogen production annually by 2030. What gaps remain in testing and certification, and what are the biggest bottlenecks?

There are two major roadblocks. The first is testing. The industry is not ready for hydrogen testing at scale. HORIBA has the facility, but many OEMs do not have these facilities, so the industry still needs to develop the capability and knowledge to test hydrogen systems.

The second is safety. Hydrogen is highly inflammable, so you have to take care of safety. At our facility in Chakan, for example, there are multiple layers of protection and other safety measures that have to be incorporated.
The government is working on it and the industry is working on it, but right now the ecosystem is not completely ready.
How long could it take India to build that hydrogen-testing readiness?
Around one to two years. The industry is working on it and the government is supporting it.
As India builds EV, hydrogen and clean-energy supply chains, where is the biggest dependence on imported technology today? Which capabilities can realistically be localised?
Batteries are still difficult. We are dependent on China. Frankly speaking, it is not only India; the whole world is dependent on China.
Testing, however, is something we can pick up relatively easily. The industry can develop those capabilities quickly.

When it comes to batteries, we really don’t know when we will be able to produce everything domestically because we do not have all the raw materials here. A very large proportion of the global raw-material supply chain is controlled by China, and that becomes a geopolitical issue as well.
But testing is different. We have the capability and the industry can develop it very fast. Maybe in six months to a year, we will be ready.
Could alternative battery technologies such as sodium-ion eventually reduce India’s dependence on imported lithium and other materials?
Many groups are working on alternatives to lithium batteries. But as of today, nobody has reached the commercial stage at the required scale.

They are still at the research stage. Much of this work is confidential, so we may not know everything that is being developed, but we have not yet seen anything commercially available that can replace lithium batteries.
For the next two to three years, I think it will remain difficult.

India has installed thousands of continuous emissions monitoring systems, but questions remain about the reliability of the data. What needs to change for that data to become more useful for enforcement?
I think you are right that it is not yet fully dependable. The data is coming in, but if you compare where we were five years ago with where we are today, it has become more and more dependable.

There is also an attitude issue. We have had a certain chalta hai and manageable attitude towards these things. But I think people are realising the importance of it and consumers are also becoming more aware.
Maybe in another two to three years, it will become much better.
Urvi Shrivastav
